title: Redwood Data Retention Demo - Bluecrest Payments
summary: Redwood demo focused on data handling and retention controls: logging redaction, PII detection, and request storage toggles via API and Console. Customer wants to know how data is retained for hosted vs dedicated/private, how to redact in-flight logging, and how to integrate KMS/SSO. Agreed next steps: share SOC2 + retention docs, run a short POC with sample traffic, and set up a follow-up technical check-in to validate redaction rules.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-06-18
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Redwood: Alex Kim, Jordan Patel, Casey Nguyen
- Bluecrest: Marta Ruiz, Ethan Cho, Priya Menon, Leo Tan

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. I'm Alex, AE on the Redwood team, with Jordan our SE and Casey from product. How's everybody doing?
[00:07] Marta Ruiz: Good, thanks. Excited to see how retention and redaction works — this is top of mind for compliance.
[00:12] Ethan Cho: Quick timeline context — we're evaluating for a pilot next month, need to understand any data leakage risk and whether requests can be disabled from storage.
[00:20] Alex Kim: Great, that's exactly what we want to cover. We'll demo the Console and API toggles, show logging redaction, and the various retention profiles. We'll also touch on dedicated/private options for data residency.
[00:32] Jordan Patel: Quick note — there might be some auto-transcript typos here, I might say K-V cache and you see K V, but, you know, t's fine.
[00:38] Priya Menon: that's fine. We'll take notes.

[02:05] Jordan Patel: All right jumping into the Console, first screen is the project settings. On the left you can see 'Data & Privacy' — this is where retention defaults live. By default hosted API request logs are retained for 30 days, but you can change to 0, 7, 30 or custom up to 365.
[02:28] Marta Ruiz: Is that per-project or per-route? We have different SLAs for fraud vs support flows.
[02:34] Jordan Patel: Good question — it's tiered. There is a project-level default and then per-route overrides. So you can set the global default to 0 and then opt-in specific routes for debugging for a short window.
[02:45] Ethan Cho: And how granular is the opt-in? Like, can we opt-in only for requests that match a certain header or tag?
[02:50] Jordan Patel: Yes — you can set tags client-side via SDK metadata or server-side via routing rules. We also support conditional retention via the Console routing rules — e.g., tag request as "debug:true" and only those will be stored under a short retention.

[05:10] Alex Kim: Now redaction — there are two layers. First at ingestion we have automated PII detection that will redact common PII patterns (credit card numbers, SSNs, emails) from logs. Second, you can define custom redaction rules with regex or use the built-in redaction templates.
[05:26] Priya Menon: How accurate is the automated PII detector? We can't rely on a black box for compliance audits.
[05:32] Jordan Patel: It's high precision for standard patterns but not perfect. Important: we provide logs showing redaction hits and the original was contributed? — sorry, the original contents are not accessible in hosted mode if you set retention to 0. For audits, we can provide metadata of redaction events and sample masked outputs.
[05:51] Priya Menon: Ok so we get an audit trail that a redaction happened but not the sensitive value — that sounds good.

[07:18] Leo Tan: For dedicated/private, how does this differ — do you still get Redwood's ingestion layer or is it customer managed?
[07:24] Casey Nguyen: In Dedicated, the control plane manages policies but data plane can be isolated. You can enable customer-managed KMS so logs are encrypted with your keys; for on-prem, you run the inference nodes and logs live in your VPC. There's also an option to disable request logging entirely at the data plane.
[07:40] Leo Tan: So we can have zero retention and keys we control?
[07:43] Casey Nguyen: Yes. With Private deployments you manage the keys and storage, Redwood's control plane handles model versions and rollouts but the persistent logs stay in your environment.

[09:05] Ethan Cho: Can you walk through the API toggle example? We want to turn off storage for all prod calls but keep it for staging.
[09:12] Jordan Patel: Sure. In the REST API there's a header x-redwood-store-requests: true|false which overrides route-level rules. So from your prod service you pass false to ensure the call is ephemeral. We also expose SDK helpers that set that header automatically when you set environment to prod.
[09:28] Marta Ruiz: Is that header authenticated? Could a client set it to false and bypass retention?
[09:33] Jordan Patel: It's honored by the ingestion layer but we also have policy enforcement — you can set an enforcement policy that disallows client-supplied overrides for certain keys. So only servers with the right service token can toggle it.

[11:00] Alex Kim: Quick demo: I'll generate a sample request with a simulated CC number and show redaction in the live logs.
[11:08] [screen share noise]
[11:12] Alex Kim: Here's a request body with card number 4111-1111-1111-1111 and email test@example.com — you'll see in the live stream those patterns are masked.
[11:25] [typing sounds]
[11:30] Jordan Patel: on the logs you can see "<redacted:card_number>" and an event recorded that matched CC pattern. There's also a column for redaction_rule_id so you can map it back to which rule triggered.
[11:44] Priya Menon: can you export these events for audit?
[11:46] Jordan Patel: Yes you can export redaction events as CSV or push them to your SIEM via webhooks. We also have an integrations doc for Splunk/Datadog.

[14:00] Marta Ruiz: For regulatory reasons we sometimes need to prove deletion — is there a hard-delete operation?
[14:06] Casey Nguyen: We support hard-delete with an async job. For hosted API, initiate a deletion request via the Console or API and we purge logs from primary stores — there's a small retention window for backup systems (up to 24 hours) for disaster recovery, but it's treated as inaccessible and encrypted. In Dedicated we can offer shorter RTO for delete with contractual SLAs.

[16:20] Ethan Cho: About encryption — we use an internal HSM for key material. Can we integrate our HSM?
[16:26] Casey Nguyen: If you're on Private or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS, yes. We have documented flows for AWS KMS/Cryptographic key usage and bring-your-own keys via HSM for on-prem. We'll share the guide.

[18:10] Priya Menon: Any SOC2 artifacts? Our procurement needs evidence.
[18:15] Alex Kim: We are SOC 2 Type II. I'll attach the SOC 2 report and our security whitepaper. Also we'll include the specific data retention and redaction sections.

[20:00] Jordan Patel: A couple of gotchas — first, alerts: if you set retention to 0 and then need to debug a production issue, you can't reconstruct requests unless you had route-level temporary capture. Second, some out-of-band logs (eg platform-level metrics) may persist longer for billing/analytics; those are aggregated and not request level.
[20:22] Marta Ruiz: How long are billing metrics kept?
[20:24] Jordan Patel: Billing aggregates are kept for 13 months by default but can be shortened. We can exclude per-customer detailed logs from those aggregates if required.

[23:00] Ethan Cho: For our pilot, we want a simple flow: prod calls never stored, staging stored 7 days, and a small sample of prod traffic allowed for debugging under strict access controls. Is that doable?
[23:12] Alex Kim: Absolutely. We can set project default to 0, enable per-route opt-in, and add a sampling rule that stores 0.1% of requests in prod to a secure retention bucket with RBAC.
[23:27] Marta Ruiz: Who can access those sample logs? We need RBAC and audit trails.
[23:30] Casey Nguyen: Access is RBAC controlled, and every read or export is logged in the audit trail with SSO principal and timestamp. We also support short-lived access tokens for forensic access.

[26:00] Priya Menon: One more question on PII detection false positives — can we provide a feedback loop to improve false positives?
[26:06] Jordan Patel: Yes, we surface false-positive flags in the Console. You can mark a match as false positive and submit it to our ML team. Over time those improve; for Dedicated we can also run a custom model trained on your labeled examples.

[28:30] Alex Kim: Quick look at the API docs — the retention endpoints are under /v1/projects/{id}/retention and /v1/routes/{id}/retention. Example payloads show header override and tag-based conditional storage.
[28:46] Ethan Cho: Any rate limits on toggles?
[28:50] Jordan Patel: No, toggles are config ops — but audit changes are rate-limited for safety.

[31:00] Marta Ruiz: Are there any differences in behavior for streaming responses? We have low-latency chat features.
[31:06] Jordan Patel: Streaming works the same; redaction happens at the chunk granularity, but there's slightly different behavior for partial tokens — we buffer to ensure we don't leak mid-token. For hosted there's a small added latency to apply redaction (tens of ms).

[33:40] Alex Kim: On cost impact: storing requests is small relative to inference cost but if you store large volumes it adds to storage costs; Redwood Optimize can recommend which routes to sample and which to fully store based on cost/latency tradeoffs.
[33:55] Casey Nguyen: Also worth noting caching/prefix caching reduces repeated tokens stored for identical prefiexes — small spelling here — prefix.

[36:10] Leo Tan: How do we prove deletion to auditors? Is there a receipt?
[36:16] Jordan Patel: We emit a deletion certificate — a signed log entry with deletion job id, timestamp, and scope. That's included in the audit export.

[38:30] Alex Kim: Let's recap next steps and I want to make sure we capture action owners.
[38:36] Marta Ruiz: Yes please.

[39:00] Alex Kim: Next steps: Alex will send SOC2 + retention docs; Jordan will run a short POC to demonstrate header toggle and redaction with sample traffic; Casey will share the Dedicated/private KMS integration guide. We'll schedule a technical check-in the week after the POC.
[39:19] Priya Menon: Sounds good. Also we'll provide sample logs and a list of high-risk routes.

[40:05] Ethan Cho: Timeline: we aim to start pilot the week of July 6.
[40:10] Alex Kim: We'll try to move fast on the POC to align.

[41:00] [wrap up small talk]
[41:15] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone, I'll follow up with the docs and the calendar invite for the POC kickoff.
[41:22] Marta Ruiz: Thanks, bye.
[41:25] Priya Menon: Thanks all.

Notes: transcript contains minor transcribe errors (e.g., K-V spelled K V, 'prefiexes' typo). Timing markers approximate and the meeting ran ~48 minutes.
